segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: After these things Jesus revealed himself again to the disciples by the Sea of Tiberias, and he revealed himself in this way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon Peter, Thomas called the Twin, Nathanael from Cana in Galilee, the sons of Zebedee, and two others of his disciples were together.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Simon Peter said to them,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “I’m going fishing.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “We’re coming with you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They went out and got into the boat, and that night they caught nothing.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Just as morning was breaking, Jesus stood on the shore; the disciples, however, did not know that it was Jesus.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Children, you don’t have any fish, do you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They answered him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “No.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Cast the net on the right side of the boat, and you will find some.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So they cast it, and now they were not strong enough to haul it in because of the great number of fish.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So that disciple whom Jesus loved said to Peter,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “It is the Lord!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Simon Peter heard that it was the Lord, he tied his outer garment around him, for he was stripped for work, and threw himself into the sea.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the other disciples came in the small boat, dragging the net full of fish, for they were not far from land, only about two hundred cubits away.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they got out on land, they saw a charcoal fire laid there, with fish lying on it, and bread.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Bring some of the fish you have just caught.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So Simon Peter went aboard and hauled the net to land, full of large fish, one hundred fifty-three of them; and though there were so many, the net was not torn.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Come and have breakfast.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: None of the disciples dared to ask him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Who are you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: They knew it was the Lord.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus came and took the bread and gave it to them, and the fish likewise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This was now the third time Jesus was revealed to the disciples after being raised from the dead.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When they had eaten breakfast, Jesus said to Simon Peter,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Simon son of John, do you love me more than these?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Feed my lambs.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him again, a second time,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Simon son of John, do you love me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Yes, Lord; you know that I love you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Shepherd my sheep.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to him the third time,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Simon son of John, do you love me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter was grieved that he said to him the third time,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you love me?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, you know everything; you know that I love you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Feed my sheep.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Truly, truly, I tell you, when you were younger, you used to fasten your own belt and walk wherever you wanted; but when you grow old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will fasten a belt around you and take you where you do not want to go.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said this to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God. And after saying this, he said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Follow me.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Peter turned and saw the disciple whom Jesus loved following—the one who had leaned back against his chest at the supper and said,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, who is it who is going to hand you over?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So when Peter saw him, he said to Jesus,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, what about him?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Jesus said to him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you? You follow me!”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So this saying spread among the brothers and sisters, that this disciple would not die. Yet Jesus did not say to him that he would not die, but,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: This is the disciple who testifies about these things and who wrote them, and we know that his testimony is true.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: There are also many other things that Jesus did; if every one of them were written down, I suppose that not even the world itself would have room for the books that would be written.

notes.note: This is another name for the Sea of Galilee, taken from the city of Tiberias on its western shore, which Herod Antipas founded and named for the emperor Tiberius. Only John’s Gospel uses this name in the New Testament.

The Greek word means something eaten as a relish with bread, which in a fishing community normally meant fish. Some translations render it more generally as “anything to eat.” The form of the question in Greek expects the answer “no.”

The word can mean fully naked, but it was also commonly used of someone wearing only an undergarment or a loincloth, as a laborer would. Most recent translations take it in this second sense here, though the older tradition has “naked.” Peter either put his outer garment on or, if he was already wearing it loosely, tucked it up to swim; the Greek allows both.
A cubit was the length of a forearm, roughly eighteen inches or forty-five centimeters. Two hundred cubits is about one hundred yards, or ninety meters.

This word occurs in only one other place in the New Testament: John 18:18, where Peter stands warming himself at a charcoal fire while he denies Jesus three times. Many interpreters think the setting is meant to recall that scene before Peter is questioned three times.
Since antiquity readers have proposed symbolic meanings for this number, but none has won general agreement. It may simply be the remembered count of an extraordinary catch.

The Greek can mean “more than these other disciples love me,” “more than you love these others,” or “more than you love these things,” meaning the boat and nets. Most interpreters prefer the first, recalling Peter’s earlier claim to greater loyalty than the rest, but the wording does not settle it.

Jesus’ first two questions use the verb agapaō and his third uses phileō, while Peter answers with phileō each time. Some interpreters see a deliberate contrast between a higher and a lesser love. Most scholars today regard the change as stylistic variation, since this Gospel uses both verbs interchangeably elsewhere and the same passage also varies its words for “know,” “feed” and “sheep.” The translation follows the majority view and uses “love” for both.

Stretching out the hands was an expression ancient writers used for crucifixion, in which the arms were spread on the crossbeam. The next verse confirms that the saying refers to Peter’s death, and early Christian tradition held that he was crucified in Rome, though the saying itself is not explicit about the manner.

Most English versions say “betray” when Judas is the subject. The Greek verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s custody, and the Gospels use the same word for what the priests and Pilate do to Jesus. The standard lexicons give “hand over” as the basic sense; many scholars regard “betray” as an inference from context, though others defend it for Judas. This translation keeps “hand over” so the repeated word remains visible.

The Greek plural was regularly used for a mixed group of men and women, and here it refers to the community of believers as a whole. Older versions have “brethren” or “brothers”; several recent ones have “brothers and sisters” or “the community.”

The “we” speaks for a group that vouches for the beloved disciple’s testimony, distinct from the disciple himself. Together with the apparent conclusion at the end of chapter 20, this leads many scholars to regard chapter 21 as an epilogue added by the disciple’s circle, though others hold it was part of the Gospel from the start. No surviving manuscript lacks the chapter.

candidates.reason: The plural used of the believing community recurs throughout Acts and the letters, and translators divide between “brothers,” “brothers and sisters” and “believers.”
Whether to distinguish it from ἀγαπάω in English affects John 5:20, 11:3, 20:2 and this passage and needs one policy.
Recurs across John, Paul and 1 John, where versions vary between “reveal,” “show,” “manifest,” “appear” and “make known.”
A key Johannine term rendered variously as “abide,” “remain,” “stay” and “live,” where variation hides a deliberate thread.
The witness vocabulary runs through John, Acts and Revelation, and “testify” versus “bear witness” should be settled together with the noun μαρτυρία.
